title: Overqualification in Singapore's resident workforce and what MOM is doing about it
asked: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo asked what overqualification means for underemployment among younger workers, women and lower-income groups, what preventative measures are in place, and how MOM assesses the impact on long-term career pathways and wage progression, including steps on job redesign, skills-based progression and workforce readiness.
response: Dr Tan See Leng said 19.4% of the resident workforce was overqualified in 2025, below the high-income countries' average of 21.6%, and that about nine in 10 of these were voluntarily overqualified. Involuntary overqualification was 1.7% and stable over the past decade, with younger, tertiary-educated workers most affected and Transportation and Storage the top sector. MOM does not track longitudinal outcomes of overqualified individuals, but median incomes of full-time employed tertiary graduates rose from $5,800 to $7,600 over 10 years. Measures cited include the merger of WSG and SSG into the Skills and Workforce Development Agency, Career Conversion Programmes, the Mid-Career Pathways Programme, herCareer for caregivers, and Job Redesign+ for flexible work arrangements.

key_points.quote: Female caregivers returning to work from a career break can also access career guidance and skills training through WSG's herCareer initiative.

key_points.quote: the fresh graduates, the mid-career workers, to the elderly workers

key_points.point: There is no single policy that covers every potential mid-career displacement; MOM also funds companies to press on with job redesign
key_points.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
key_points.quote: There is not a particular, single policy that we can introduce that would be a panacea to cover every single potential mid-career displacement.

left_open: Which indicators MOM uses to determine whether overqualification is becoming persistent rather than transitional.
What thresholds would trigger further intervention.
How long-term wage and career progression outcomes are tracked for younger graduates who remain overqualified for extended periods.
Whether overqualification today affects readiness for emerging roles tomorrow, and how that risk is mitigated.
Whether employers hold bias against workers who take a career break, and whether caregivers can return to their previous role.
supplementary: Supplementary questions covered how persistent overqualification is measured, caregiver return-to-work support, youth internship access and help for mismatched mid-career workers.
